# Digest R8 — 2 Pet 3:8–18 (L3440–3606)

**Source:** Gene L. Green, *Jude and 2 Peter* (BECNT)  
**Range file:** `R8-2pet-3_8-18.txt`  
**Line range:** L3440–3606  
**Tags:** `2-peter`, `gene-green`, `new-creation`, `paul-apostle`, `green-jude-2peter-becnt`

## Coverage

Read in full (L3440–3606): Green’s exegesis of **2 Pet 3:8–18**, covering:

- **3:8–10** — Ps 90:4 and divine vs. human time; delay as patience toward repentance (not Epicurean refutation of judgment); day of the Lord as thief; cosmic conflagration of heavens/elements/earth; **εὑρεθήσεται** = judicial discovery of works (text-critical note on “found” / “in the night”).
- **3:11–13** — Ethics from eschatology; holy/dutiful living; expecting and *hastening* the day of God; **renewal not annihilation** — new heavens and new earth where righteousness dwells (Isa 65:17 / 66:22).
- **3:14–18a** — Diligence to be found blameless; forbearance as salvation; **Paul as beloved brother**, writings according to given wisdom; Pauline corpus; “some things hard to understand”; ignorant/unstable twist Paul **as even the other Scriptures** → Paul’s letters classified as Scripture; destruction; guard against lawless error; grow in grace and knowledge.
- **3:18b** — Doxology to **Jesus Christ** (high Christology); glory now and into the day of eternity; Amen (text-critical note).
- Section intros L3489–3491, L3531–3533, L3585–3587; additional notes L3479–3483, L3521–3525, L3599–3601.

**Not read:** material outside this cache slice.

## Claims

### 3:8–10 day/1000 years; day of the Lord; elements

**C1.** Green attributes to Peter a response to the false teachers’ doubt (3:4: “Where is the promise of his coming?… all things remain as they were from the beginning of creation”): apparent delay argues against the coming and its judgment.
- Quote: “Peter now responds to the question that the false teachers have raised in order to sow doubt… According to the heretics, the apparent delay in the coming of the Lord argues strongly against the reality of this event with its attendant judgment.”
- Locus: L3446

**C2.** Green: “Beloved” marks transition and draws readers into solidarity with Peter against heretics who willfully neglected facts about creation, providence, and judgment (3:5).
- Quote: “Peter addresses his readers as ‘Beloved’… draws the readers into the circle with himself while arguing that they should not be like the heretics, who have willfully neglected the facts about God’s creation, providence, and judgment (3:5).”
- Locus: L3446

**C3.** Green: same verb as 3:5 contrasts heretics’ ignoring with what recipients must not let escape notice; believers guided by biblical teaching, heretics by perceptions alone.
- Quote: “The contrast between the believers and the heretics is marked by the use of the same verb in this verse and in verse 5. … The believers are informed by biblical teaching while the heretics rely only on their perceptions (3:4). Theology should guide the church and not specious historical argument.”
- Locus: L3446

**C4.** Green: 3:8 alludes to **Ps. 90:4 [89:4 LXX]** (“For a thousand years in your sight are as the yesterday that is past, and as a watch in the night”).
- Quote: “The second part of the verse alludes to Ps. 90:4 [89:4 LXX], which in the LXX states: ‘For a thousand years in your sight are as the yesterday that is past, and as a watch in the night’…”
- Locus: L3448

**C5.** Green: Psalm 90 contrasts God’s judgment and life’s transitoriness with God’s eternal nature; Peter’s use encourages right conduct in light of life’s transitoriness (Ps 90:12; cf. 2 Pet 3:11).
- Quote: “The psalm speaks of the judgment of God that comes upon humanity… and the transitory nature of life… in contrast with the eternal nature of God (v. 4). Peter’s use of the psalm is consonant with its purpose to encourage right conduct in light of the transitoriness of life (Ps. 90:12; cf. 2 Pet. 3:11).”
- Locus: L3448

**C6.** Green notes Jewish development (Jub. 4.30; 2 En. 33.1–2; Gen. Rab. 19.8; 22.1) and later Christian “six days = six thousand years” (Barn. 15.4; Irenaeus), with Barnabas’s form close to 2 Pet 3:8 and possibly influenced by this letter.
- Quote: “Psalm 90 was the impetus for the development in Jewish thought that ‘one day’ was a way to speak figuratively of ‘a thousand years’… After the first century, the same math appeared in the theology of the church… The form of the citation in Barnabas is close to 2 Pet. 3:8 and may have been influenced by this letter…”
- Locus: L3450

**C7. [CRITICAL — not millennial key]** Green rejects reading 3:8 as interpretive key equating “days” with “a thousand years” (or vice versa, incl. Rev 20:2–7).
- Quote: “However, we should not interpret 2 Pet. 3:8 along these lines. Peter does not forward an interpretive key by which we may understand certain ‘days’ in God’s plan as if they represent ‘a thousand years,’ or even understand references to ‘a thousand years’ as if this period means ‘one day’ (Rev. 20:2–7).”
- Locus: L3452

**C8.** Green: Ps 90:4 explains 3:9 (“The Lord is not slow…”); divine perspective on time ≠ human; prolonged by human standards can be brief by divine calculation; Peter does **not relativize time** but affirms different criteria for “rapid” and “slow” (contra Käsemann).
- Quote: “His argument is simply that the divine perspective on time is not the same as the human perspective. A period that may appear prolonged by human standards is actually brief according to divine calculation. … Peter does not relativize time but simply affirms that the criteria for ‘rapid’ and ‘slow’ are different for humans and God (contra Käsemann 1982: 193–94).”
- Locus: L3452

**C9.** Green on 3:9: “The Lord is not slow to fulfill the promise” answers false teachers who “count slowness”; builds on 3:8; “promise” = Christ’s coming (3:4) with judgment (3:7, 10, 12) and new world (3:13).
- Quote: “Peter affirms… ‘The Lord is not slow to fulfill the promise’ as a response to the opinion of the false teachers… The ‘promise’ Peter has in mind is that of Christ’s coming (3:4 and comments) with its attendant judgment (3:7, 10, 12) and promise of the new world (3:13).”
- Locus: L3454

**C10.** Green: OT/Jewish topos of divine delay in judgment or salvation (Deut 7:10; Hab 2:3; Isa 46:13; 2 Bar. 20.1–6; Sir. 35:19); Peter insists judgment will come, but—unlike Sirach’s denial of patient mercy—**delay is due to divine mercy**.
- Quote: “Peter is concerned precisely about this issue: God’s judgment will indeed come. But in contrast with 2 Pet. 3:9b, Sirach declares that God will not show mercy by turning aside from judgment. Peter emphasizes that the delay in judgment is due to divine mercy.”
- Locus: L3456

**C11.** Green situates delay-skepticism in first-century philosophical debate: Epicurean non-providence, denial of predictive prophecy and judgment; Plutarch records delay (βραδύτης) as “the most telling argument” against providence (Mor. 548C, 549B); Paul at Athens (Acts 17:18, 31).
- Quote: “At the heart of Epicurean philosophy was the notion that the gods, if indeed they existed at all, are not providentially engaged in the workings of the world. … Since the gods were removed from the world, there was therefore neither divine providence nor any divine judgment, past or future. … ‘The delay [βραδύτης, bradytēs] and procrastination of the Deity in punishing the wicked appears to me the most telling argument by far’ (The Delay of Divine Judgment, in Mor. 548C).”
- Locus: L3458–L3460

**C12.** Green: hard to imagine Epicureans at church table, yet Epicurean tenets were common currency; delay-question is **not a specific identity marker** for the heretics—common Jewish and Mediterranean topos; heretics’ beliefs eclectic.
- Quote: “In the end, the question about the delay in divine judgment is not a marker to identify specifically who these heretics are since, as noted above, this was a common topos both within Judaism… and in the wider Mediterranean world. The heretics appear to have an eclectic admixture of beliefs…”
- Locus: L3462

**C13.** Green: true reason for delay = God “is patient toward you, not willing for anyone to perish but all to come to repentance”; delay does not argue against judgment’s reality but evidences patience; patience ≠ tolerance—ends in terrible judgment day (3:10).
- Quote: “According to our author, the delay in judgment does not argue against its reality but is rather evidence that God ‘is patient toward you’… But this patience should not be confused with tolerance toward sin, because God’s patience will come to an end in the terrible day of judgment (3:10…)”
- Locus: L3464

**C14.** Green: “toward you” stretches hand publicly to those tempted or beginning to follow false teachers (2:14, 18).
- Quote: “Somewhat surprisingly, Peter notes that God is patient ‘toward you.’ With these words, which will be read publicly during the gatherings of the believers, Peter stretches out the hand to those who are tempted to follow or who have begun to follow the way of the false teachers (2:14, 18).”
- Locus: L3464

**C15. [CRITICAL — not universalism]** Green: God not willing anyone perish eternally; desire “all come to repentance” (// 1 Tim 2:4) **does not imply universal salvation**—following verse makes clear; repentance = abandon sin, turn to God, do works evidencing repentance.
- Quote: “This does not imply that Peter believes in universal salvation, as the following verse makes clear. Rather, God wants ‘all to come to repentance.’ … This ‘repentance’… is the act of abandoning deeds associated with sin (Heb. 6:1), turning to God (Acts 20:21), and doing works that provide evidence of ‘repentance’…”
- Locus: L3466

**C16.** Green on 3:10: despite apparent delay (v. 9), “the day of the Lord will come”—eschatological appearance, judgment, wrath against unrepentant; also day of salvation for God’s people, but **Peter’s focus is terror**; may be “day of the Lord Jesus.”
- Quote: “‘The day of the Lord’ is the eschatological moment when God will appear, judge the inhabitants of the earth, and pour out his wrath against the unrepentant because of their sin… Although this will also be a day of salvation for God’s people… Peter’s focus is on the terror of that event.”
- Locus: L3468

**C17.** Green: day comes unexpectedly “as a thief”; roots in Jesus’ teaching (Matt 24:43–44; Luke 12:39–40), then church instruction (1 Thess 5:2; Rev 3:3; 16:15); Peter **omits** “in the night”; need not assume direct dependence on Paul (3:15–16) given common knowledge of dominical teaching.
- Quote: “The assertion that the coming will be ‘as a thief in the night’ finds its roots in the teaching of Jesus… Peter, however, omits the note about the thief coming ‘in the night’… We need not assume that Peter draws directly from Paul (3:15–16; cf. Neyrey 1993: 242) given the common knowledge of this dominical teaching.”
- Locus: L3470

**C18.** Green: heavens and earth, created/sustained by God (3:5–7), **will be destroyed by him before new heavens and earth** (3:13); heavens pass with a “roar” (ῥοιζηδόν rare)—thunder of judgment and/or sound of intense fire.
- Quote: “The heavens and the earth, created and sustained by God (3:5–7), will be destroyed by him before the new heavens and earth are ushered in (3:13). … he may have in mind the ‘thunder’ that accompanies the judgment of God… On the other hand, he may be thinking of nothing other than the sound generated by intense fire (3:7, 12).”
- Locus: L3472

**C19.** Green on στοιχεῖα: not celestial bodies or supernatural powers (as in Gal/Col) but **totality of material of the world**—contrasted with “heavens” in 3:12; corresponds to “heavens and the earth” (3:7); final clause identifies elements with “the earth”; fire-destruction of earth favored by biblical tradition; **more indebted to biblical/Jewish/Christian tradition than Stoic conflagration** (cf. 3:7).
- Quote: “In 3:12 these ‘elements’ are placed in contrast with ‘the heavens,’ and they should therefore be understood as the totality of the material of the world. … Once again, though Peter’s readers are likely familiar with Stoic doctrine concerning a coming conflagration, Peter’s thought is more likely indebted to the biblical, Jewish, and Christian traditions regarding the end (see 3:7 and comments).”
- Locus: L3474

**C20. [CRITICAL — “found” / judicial discovery, not mere burning of works]** Green: final clause καὶ γῆ καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ ἔργα εὑρεθήσεται = “even the earth and the works that are **discovered** in it”; εὑρεθήσεται (as in v. 14) suggests **judicial inquiry**—God discovers deeds and judges; passive = divine agency; nothing/no one escapes wrath save those who embrace salvation (3:15).
- Quote: “The verb εὑρεθήσεται in this context, as in verse 14, suggests a judicial inquiry through which God will discover the deeds of humanity and will execute his judgment on the basis of what he finds… The passive voice of the verb here suggests the divine agency in this inquiry. … Peter faces off against them, declaring that nothing and no one will escape God’s wrath save for those who embrace the salvation of God (2 Pet. 3:15). ‘The works’ of those who do evil will be discovered.”
- Locus: L3476

### 3:11–13 living toward new heavens and earth

**C21.** Green’s section frame: delay relative to God’s vs. human time and grows from divine mercy (3:8–9); fierce fiery judgment and destruction of all things will come (3:10); now final judgment calls to **holy and dutiful life** (3:11) knowing end brings **new heaven and earth characterized by righteousness** (3:12–13); Peter joins **eschatology and ethics** against heretics’ dissolution of the two.
- Quote: “The final judgment is a call to live a holy and dutiful life (3:11), knowing that the end will bring not only destruction but also a new order in God’s creation—a new heaven and new earth—which will be characterized by righteousness (3:12–13). Peter joins together eschatology and ethics as a counter to the heretics’ dissolution of the two.”
- Locus: L3491

**C22.** Green: Peter does not speculate on timing of eschatological events; final events motivate Christian conduct; false teachers’ skepticism founded immoral teaching; for Peter, terrible reality of judgment is fundamental ethical motivation.
- Quote: “Our author does not engage in speculation about the timing of forthcoming eschatological events. He rather sees the final events of the world described above as motivation for Christian conduct. … They understand the delay in judgment as an excuse to embrace an immoral lifestyle. Peter, on the other hand, affirms the terrible reality of coming judgment, and this then becomes a fundamental motivation in his ethics.”
- Locus: L3502

**C23.** Green: λύω summarizes final judgment when the world as known will be destroyed; despite assize, hope comes (3:13); question ποταπούς has **imperatival force**—“You ought to live in a holy and dutiful way!”; δεῖ marks necessity not option.
- Quote: “Although Peter asks a question that begins with the interrogative ποταπούς… the sentence has imperatival force: ‘You ought to live in a holy and dutiful way!’ Peter regards such conduct not as an option but as a necessity, marked in this clause by the term δεῖ…”
- Locus: L3502–L3504

**C24.** Green: conduct = holy (not immoral like false teachers) and devoted in duty to God (εὐσεβείαις), already described in 1:3–11; eschatological expectation leads to holy conduct as skepticism led to immorality.
- Quote: “Peter describes the conduct that should mark the believers in anticipation of the end as holy… not immoral like that of the false teachers… and as devoted in duty to God… Just as eschatological skepticism has led to immorality, so eschatological expectation leads to holy conduct marked by devotion in duty to God.”
- Locus: L3506

**C25.** Green: last day brings cosmic destruction **and** promise of new heaven/earth and truly just society; readers called to **expecting and hastening** the coming of the day of God; προσδοκάω = firm expectation, not mere “hope for.”
- Quote: “But it also carries the promise of the coming of a new heaven and new earth and the inauguration of a truly just society (3:13). Therefore… Peter calls his readers to… expecting and hastening the coming of the day of God… The verb προσδοκάω… does not mean simply ‘hope for’… but rather suggests firm expectation or sure hope with expectation of fulfillment…”
- Locus: L3508

**C26. [CRITICAL — hastening]** Green: σπεύδω transitive—“to hasten” the coming (object = τὴν παρουσίαν); because God retards judgment for repentance (3:9), **repentance accelerates** “the coming of the day of God”; God effects acceleration with reference to human repentance (// Jewish texts; later rabbinic).
- Quote: “The second verb, σπεύδω… is not intransitive here… but… is instead transitive, ‘to hasten’ something. Because God retards his judgment due to his desire that sinners should repent (3:9), this repentance will accelerate ‘the coming of the day of God’… Although God is the one who effects the acceleration, he brings it to pass with reference to human repentance…”
- Locus: L3510

**C27.** Green: παρουσία here = coming of the “day of God,” same event as “day of the Lord” in 3:10 (not only advent of Christ as usual); heavens destroyed by fire; elements melted by burning; **“The end is not for fear but for hope.”**
- Quote: “The παρουσία… is commonly the advent of Christ… but here the expectation is the coming of the ‘day of God,’ the same event described as ‘the day of the Lord’ in 3:10… Although this will be the end of the present heaven and earth, the believers hold a glorious hope, as Peter explains in the next verse. The end is not for fear but for hope.”
- Locus: L3510–L3512

**C28. [CRITICAL — new-creation: renewal not annihilation]** Green: despite destructive judgment, **Christian hope is renovation of creation, not its annihilation**; as flood-destroyed ancient world (2:5; 3:6) gave way to present order, present world suffers judgment (3:7) then God ushers in new creation.
- Quote: “In spite of the destructive forces of the divine judgment (3:7, 10–12), the Christian hope is the renovation of creation and not its annihilation. As the ancient world destroyed by the flood (2:5; 3:6) gave way to the present order, so also the present world will suffer divine judgment (3:7), but in turn God will usher in the new creation.”
- Locus: L3514

**C29.** Green: expectation κατὰ τὸ ἐπάγγελμα αὐτοῦ—the promise heretics put in doubt (3:4); first-person plural places churches in solidarity with Peter and prophetic witness.
- Quote: “Peter affirms that he and the believers (note the first-person plural) expect… a reality beyond the final judgment because of… his promise, the very promise that the heretics have put in doubt (3:4 and comments). Peter places the churches in solidarity with himself and the prophetic witness regarding this expectation.”
- Locus: L3514

**C30.** Green: promise specifically **Isa. 65:17**, repeated in **66:22** (“new heavens and a new earth”); hope vivid in Jewish apocalyptic and primitive church (Rom 8:19–21; Rev 21:1); created order not eternal but subject to change; should bring hope not despair; Peter resonates with eschatological hope that **destruction is followed by renewal**.
- Quote: “The ‘promise’ that Peter has in mind is specifically that of Isa. 65:17, repeated in 66:22… The created order is not eternal but is subject to upheaval and change… yet this should bring hope rather than despair since God the Creator will inaugurate a new order. … Peter resonates with the eschatological hope that destruction is followed by renewal.”
- Locus: L3516

**C31.** Green: new order embraces moral order; new heaven/earth **ἐν οἷς δικαιοσύνη κατοικεῖ**—in contrast to present world of evil deeds (3:10b); false teachers rejected “way of righteousness” (2:21) and with followers will be **excluded**; in that world no sin/injustice.
- Quote: “The new heaven and new earth, in contrast with the present world filled with evil deeds (see 3:10b), will be one… ‘in which dwells righteousness.’ … These people and their followers will be excluded from the ‘new heavens and a new earth’ because in these only ‘dwells righteousness.’ … In that new world, there will be no sin, no injustice. All will be just and will act in justice toward their fellows.”
- Locus: L3518

### 3:14–18a diligence; Paul; final warning

**C32.** Green’s closing frame: exhortations—be diligent morally (v. 14); regard delay as sign of salvation (v. 15); guard against falling (v. 17); grow in knowledge and grace (v. 18a); heretics twist Paul’s writings and “other Scriptures” → own destruction; Peter distances them from Paul, draws Paul into his circle.
- Quote: “In bringing the letter to a close, Peter gives his readers a series of exhortations… In the midst of these summary exhortations, Peter turns once again to counter the heretics, noting the way they twist Paul’s writings and the ‘other Scriptures,’ a move that spells their own destruction (vv. 15b–16). … While they try to evoke Paul’s writings in support of their views, Peter distances them from Paul while drawing Paul into his own circle.”
- Locus: L3533

**C33.** Green on 3:14: point of departure = final judgment (3:10–12) and new creation (3:13); eschatology not speculation or escape from responsibility but motivation to preserve moral life; deeds judged (3:10); only the just enter new order (3:13).
- Quote: “Eschatology is not a topic of speculation for Peter, nor an excuse to escape from responsibility, but rather a motivation to preserve the moral life. Human deeds will be judged by God (3:10), who will establish a new order into which only the just shall enter (3:13).”
- Locus: L3544

**C34.** Green: σπουδάσατε “be diligent” (favorite urgency term, 1:10, 15) **to be found** blameless; εὑρίσκω again = God’s judicial inquiry (as 3:10); before him (αὐτῷ) ἄσπιλοι and ἀμώμητοι—negative of false teachers as “spots and defects” (2:13); imitate lamb without defect/blemish (1 Pet 1:19)—point of contact with 1 Peter (2 Pet 3:1); “in peace” = objective reconciliation/acceptability before God, not mere emotional tranquillity.
- Quote: “As in 3:10, the verb εὑρίσκω… refers to God’s judicial inquiry into the deeds of humanity… In 3:14 Peter employs the negative form of these terms… to emphasize his call that the believers should in no wise adopt the conduct of the heretics. … This ‘peace’ is not some form of emotional tranquillity but rather the objective condition of being reconciled with God (Rom. 5:1) and being found acceptable before him…”
- Locus: L3546

**C35.** Green on 3:15: return to 3:9—consider forbearance of our Lord **as salvation**; Peter and false teachers evaluate empirical evidence differently; μακροθυμία = God’s patience toward sinners, not procrastination; salvation here = rescue from coming wrath (3:10–12) **and entrance into new righteous world** (3:13).
- Quote: “And consider the forbearance of our Lord as salvation… Peter urges them to properly evaluate ‘the forbearance of our Lord’… which is God’s patience toward sinful humans and not his procrastination… In the present context salvation includes rescue from the coming wrath of God (3:10–12) and entrance into his new righteous world (3:13).”
- Locus: L3548

**C36.** Green: Peter mentions Paul because false teachers distorted his message and used epistles to support heresy; possible they identify as followers of “Paul, the apostle of liberty” (freedom also common in ancient philosophy, 2:19); Peter seeks complete harmony with Paul in teaching and personal relationship.
- Quote: “The reason Peter needs to mention Paul’s letters is because the false teachers have distorted their message and have used those epistles to support their heresy (3:16b). It is possible that the heretics identify themselves as followers of Paul, the apostle of liberty… Due to the false teachers’ appeal to Paul, Peter seeks to show the complete harmony between himself and the apostle to the gentiles, not only with respect to his teaching but also in their personal relationship.”
- Locus: L3550

**C37.** Green: despite Gal 2:11–21 rebuke and Tübingen debates, **here no evidence of a breach**; Paul called “our beloved brother”—profound love and solidarity; brother in faith and colleague in gospel service.
- Quote: “Although the relationship between Paul and Peter has been a topic of considerable debate, especially since the time of Baur and the Tübingen School (Harris 1975), here there is no evidence of a breach between them. Our author calls Paul ‘our beloved brother.’ With the adjective ‘beloved’… Peter expresses his profound love for and solidarity with Paul.”
- Locus: L3550

**C38.** Green: Paul wrote to Asia Minor congregations (likely some recipients of this letter and 1 Peter); impossible to determine with certainty which letters from comparison; location suggests Galatians, Ephesians (if circular), Colossians, lost Laodiceans (Col 4:16).
- Quote: “It is impossible to determine with any certainty which letters our author has in mind on the basis of a comparison between the Pauline corpus and 2 Peter (as Bauckham 1983: 320 correctly notes). But the location of the readers in Asia Minor suggests that some may know letters such as Galatians, Ephesians… Colossians, and the lost correspondence to the Laodiceans (Col. 4:16).”
- Locus: L3552

**C39.** Green: Paul wrote **according to the wisdom given to him**—divine wisdom, not mere savvy, tied to right conduct; **marks Paul’s writings as inspired**, not merely human origin, confirmed next verse; consonant with Paul’s own affirmations (1 Cor 2:3–7; Col 1:28).
- Quote: “Peter displays profound respect for Paul, recognizing that he wrote… according to the wisdom that was given to him… Peter’s affirmation of the wisdom that God granted Paul marks Paul’s writings as inspired and not simply of human origin, a point confirmed in the following verse.”
- Locus: L3552

**C40.** Green on 3:16: 3:15 = letters to Asia Minor; 3:16 = content of **“all his letters”**—implies collection/Pauline corpus already existing when Peter pens; copying/collecting common (E. Richards)—**not** proof 2 Peter is postapostolic.
- Quote: “the present verse implies that the churches have collected his writings and that at the time when Peter pens this missive, some form of the Pauline corpus was already in existence. … so that we cannot assume that the existence of a ‘Pauline corpus’ is a sign that 2 Peter comes to us from the postapostolic era…”
- Locus: L3554

**C41.** Green: Paul spoke “concerning these matters”—what the church expects (3:14), e.g. coming judgment (3:12) and new creation (3:13); affirms unity of Peter’s theology with Paul; **negates** false teachers’ claim of solidarity with Paul.
- Quote: “In these writings… the apostle to the gentiles spoke ‘concerning these matters’… the ‘matters’ that the church expects (3:14), such as the coming judgment (3:12) and the new creation (3:13…). With these words, Peter affirms the unity between the theology that he teaches and that of Paul, while at the same time negating the claim of the false teachers…”
- Locus: L3554

**C42. [CRITICAL — hard to understand]** Green: in Paul’s letters “some things hard to understand” (δυσνόητά τινα)—not everything; heretics’ problem is **not** difficulty of interpretation but **distortion** (στρεβλοῦσιν) by the “ignorant and unstable” (false teachers 2:12; 3:5 and their weak disciples 2:14); wrench true into false.
- Quote: “Yet Peter does not affirm that everything within Paul’s writings is hard to understand but rather only ‘some things’ (τινα, tina). However, the problem of the false teachers is not the difficulty of interpreting the message that God gave Paul. Rather, the heretics have distorted his teaching… These people ‘twist’… Paul’s teaching, wrenching and distorting it in such a way that the true is turned into the false…”
- Locus: L3556

**C43.** Green: Pauline distortions known from Paul himself—grace/antinomianism (Rom 3:8; 3:21–27; 5:20; 1 Cor 6:12; Gal 5:13; cf. Jude 4) and eschatology (2 Thess 2:2–3; 2 Tim 2:17–18); heretics’ distortions concern **precisely these two points** (2:19; 3:4).
- Quote: “From Paul’s own writings we are aware that some in his audience distorted his preaching concerning grace… as support of antinomianism… Others also perverted his teaching regarding eschatological events… The Pauline doctrines that the ‘ignorant and unstable’ have distorted have to do with precisely these two points (2:19; 3:4).”
- Locus: L3556

**C44. [CRITICAL — Paul = Scripture]** Green: they twist Paul “as even the other Scriptures”; “Scriptures” = OT (2 Pet 1:20–21 etc.); early expansion to Jesus’ teaching (1 Tim 5:18); here Peter **takes a further step**, calling OT “the other Scriptures,” **implying Paul’s letters are classified as “Scripture”** (λοιπάς = those apart from what is referred to).
- Quote: “They twist his teaching… ‘as even the other Scriptures.’ … In the present verse, Peter takes one step further in the development of the canon, calling the writings of the OT ‘the other Scriptures.’ Peter here implies that Paul’s letters are classified as ‘Scripture’ as well…”
- Locus: L3558

**C45.** Green: if 2 Peter authentic, this is **ad hoc broadening** of “Scripture” via this lexeme; not indefensible given apostolic authority; early fathers’ ascriptions of NT as Scripture not lavish but not absent; **dating 2 Peter to early second century on basis of 3:16 outstrips the evidence**.
- Quote: “If we regard 2 Peter as an authentic work of the apostle, then this categorization of Paul’s writings as ‘Scripture’ is an ad hoc broadening of the concept communicated via this lexeme. … Dating 2 Peter as a document written in the early second century on the basis of 3:16 outstrips the evidence…”
- Locus: L3558

**C46.** Green: distorting Scripture (Paul, Jesus, or OT) leads **to their own destruction** (ἀπώλεια); problem not poorly understanding portions of revelation but using twisted interpretation to **justify immorality**; twisted teaching and practice hand in hand; heretical teaching → moral decadence.
- Quote: “The problem of the false teachers is not that they have poorly understood portions of divine revelation but that they use their twisted interpretation to justify their immorality… Twisted teaching and twisted practice go hand in hand. Heretical teaching has led to moral decadence.”
- Locus: L3560

**C47.** Green on 3:17: emphatic Ὑμεῖς + “beloved” contrasts readers with heretics; προγινώσκοντες ≠ “knowing this first” (Peter uses πρῶτον γινώσκω for that, 1:20; 3:3) and **not** testamentary fiction of future heretics; heretics already active (2:13–14, 18; 3:16); readers not yet succumbed, have advance apostolic/prophetic warning—so guard (φυλάσσεσθε = guard against/avoid).
- Quote: “We should not understand προγινώσκοντες… as a reference to a future advent of the heretics… Rather, since the recipients of this letter have not yet succumbed to the error and since they already have in hand the apostolic argument against the error via this letter as well as the prophetic and apostolic teaching regarding the coming error (3:2–3), they are advised in advance and can guard themselves from the heresy…”
- Locus: L3564

**C48.** Green: danger is social as well as doctrinal—“carried away” by others’ opinion (// Barnabas, Gal 2:13); “lawless” as Sodom (2:7)—refuse any moral law; πλάνῃ emphasizes conduct with false teaching (2:18), not only deceptive doctrine; warn against **apostasy**—do not fall from “own firm position” founded on prophetic and apostolic revelation.
- Quote: “The problem Peter faces is not only doctrinal but also social. It is quite easy to be ‘carried away’… by the opinion of others… Peter warns against the sin of apostasy… Peter’s earnest desire is that they stay firm in the teaching that is founded on the prophetic and apostolic revelation, and not follow after the deceptive and corrupting error of the false teachers and thereby come into ruin.”
- Locus: L3566–L3568

**C49.** Green on 3:18a: best antidote against apostasy = growing Christian life; grow in grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ—for whole congregation not only neophytes; moral growth already 1:5–7; grace = advances in appropriation/experience of salvation benefits (Kelly: favor); **knowledge personal**, object = Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; with grace, strongest antidote against false teachers’ lures.
- Quote: “The apostle recognizes that the best antidote against apostasy is a Christian life that is growing. … Such knowledge, which marked the believers’ conversion, also continues and increases throughout the life of the Christian. Along with grace, such knowledge is the strongest antidote against the destructive lures of the false teachers.”
- Locus: L3570

### 3:18b doxology

**C50.** Green: body closing ends 3:18a; **3:18b** is less-elaborate letter closing ascribing honor to Jesus Christ throughout eternity.
- Quote: “The body closing of the letter came to its conclusion in 3:18a. The final doxology in 3:18b serves as a less-than-elaborate letter closing, which ascribes honor to Jesus Christ throughout eternity.”
- Locus: L3587

**C51. [CRITICAL — high Christology]** Green: doxology **to Jesus Christ**—one of very few NT doxologies specifically to Christ (// 2 Tim 4:18; Rev 1:5–6); evidence of Peter’s high Christology, also in 3:18a and letter opening (titles God, Savior, Lord, 1:1–2; cf. Jude 25).
- Quote: “The majority of the doxologies in the NT are dedicated to God the Father. This doxology is one of the very few dedicated specifically to Jesus Christ… Its presence at the end of this letter provides evidence of Peter’s high Christology. His high Christology is suggested in the first part of this verse as well as at the beginning of this letter, where he ascribes to Christ the divine titles ‘God,’ ‘Savior,’ and ‘Lord’…”
- Locus: L3596

**C52.** Green: glory is his “now”—all should honor him with conduct and faithfulness presently (unlike false teachers’ regard for celestial beings, 2:10); endures “into the day of eternity”; anticipated “day” destroys present order (3:10, 12) and inaugurates eternal new era (1:19; 3:13); final amen frames present situation by Christ’s eternal honor—foundation for standing firm.
- Quote: “This ‘glory’… is his ‘now’… and therefore all should honor him with their conduct and faithfulness at the present time… The honor ascribed to him now will endure ‘into the day of eternity’… The ‘day’ that Peter and his readers anticipate will signal the destruction of the present order (3:10, 12) and will also inaugurate a new era that will last throughout eternity (1:19; 3:13). With his vision fixed on that hope, he utters the final ‘amen’…”
- Locus: L3596

### Additional Notes / text-critical (3:10 “found”)

**C53.** Green, add. note 3:10: some MSS/versions add “in the night” (ἐν νυκτί; C 𝔐 vgmss syh; cf. 1 Thess 5:2); **absent from principal witnesses** (𝔓72 א A B Ψ).
- Quote: “Unsurprisingly, some MSS and versions include the words ‘in the night’ (ἐν νυκτί, en nykti, in C 𝔐 vgmss syh; cf. 1 Thess. 5:2), although they are absent from the principal witnesses (𝔓72 א A B Ψ).”
- Locus: L3481

**C54. [CRITICAL — text of 3:10 εὑρεθήσεται]** Green: reading εὑρεθήσεται (“will be discovered”) has **strong textual support** (א B P); 𝔓72 adds λυόμενα (“will be found dissolved”); various scribal clarifications lack strong early witness; critical-text reading is **the more difficult one** (see commentary = judicial discovery, C20).
- Quote: “The reading εὑρεθήσεται (heurethēsetai, will be discovered) enjoys strong textual support (א B P), although 𝔓72 adds λυόμενα (lyomena, ‘will be found dissolved’). Various other readings appear in the scribal attempt to clarify the sense although none has strong early witness. The reading as here presented and in the critical texts is indeed the more difficult one. See the commentary.”
- Locus: L3483

**C55.** Green, add. notes 3:11: οὕτως (𝔓72 B 614 1739) vs easier οὖν (א A Ψ 048)—easier may be scribal; pronoun ὑμᾶς vs ἡμᾶς vs **no pronoun** (𝔓72,74 B)—UBS4/NA27 bracket ὑμᾶς, editors uncertain.
- Quote: “While the MS evidence is not decisive in either direction, the reading οὖν (oun) is the easier to understand, lending support to the idea that it may have been a scribal addition. … The papyri (𝔓72, 74) as well as B, however, include no pronoun at this point. The decision is difficult and left the editors of the critical texts (UBS4, NA27) uncertain…”
- Locus: L3523–L3525

**C56.** Green, add. note 3:18: final ἀμήν absent in B 1241 1243; inclusion in 𝔓72 א A C P Ψ 33 and 𝔐 **argues strongly in favor of inclusion**.
- Quote: “Although the final ἀμήν (amēn) does not appear in B 1241 1243, its inclusion in 𝔓72 א A C P Ψ 33 as well as 𝔐 argues strongly in favor of its inclusion.”
- Locus: L3601
